title: A Solar Probe of Dark Matter Decay in the Galaxy
summary: Dark matter (DM) particles decaying in the Galactic halo can inject energetic $e^\pm$ that inverse-Compton scatter (ICS) solar photons into $γ$-rays, producing a diffuse and extended halo of emission around the Sun. We present the first quantitative study of this signal as an indirect probe of decaying DM. The intense solar photon field in the inner heliosphere amplifies the inverse-Compton emissivity by many orders of magnitude relative to the interstellar radiation field, making the Sun an unusually sensitive local converter of sunlight into $γ$-rays via scattering with injected $e^\pm$. Using 15 years of Fermi-LAT solar-halo data, we derive stringent limits on the DM lifetime for 10 GeV-10TeV masses at the level of $τ_χ\sim 10^{27}\,\mathrm{s}$ in leptonic decay channels. The predicted surface brightness rises steeply toward the Sun, and the $γ$-ray flux falls off at high energy due to Klein-Nishina suppression. Solar ICS $γ$-rays measured with degree scale angular resolution therefore provide a novel and complementary probe of DM decays, adding a local $γ$-ray search channel that is systematically distinct from both Galactic diffuse analyses and direct charged-particle measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper uses gamma-rays from solar inverse-Compton scattering of dark matter decay products to set new constraints on dark matter lifetimes, highlighting the Sun as a unique local probe for decaying dark matter.
AI.motivation: To explore a novel indirect detection method for decaying dark matter (DM) through solar inverse-Compton (ICS) gamma-ray emission.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of ICS gamma-rays produced by energetic electrons and positrons from DM decay scattering solar photons, using 15 years of Fermi-LAT solar-halo data.
AI.result: Derived stringent limits on DM lifetime (~10^{27} seconds) for masses between 10 GeV and 10 TeV in leptonic decay channels, identifying a strong surface brightness increase toward the Sun and energy-dependent flux suppression due to Klein-Nishina effects.
AI.conclusion: Solar ICS gamma-rays provide a sensitive and complementary probe for decaying DM, distinct from Galactic diffuse gamma-ray and charged particle searches, leveraging the amplified solar photon field as a local converter.

title: Searching for unresolved massive black hole pairs through AGN photometric variability
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, Accepted for publication by A&A
summary: Since their discovery, AGN light curves are known to be intrinsically variable. In the optical/UV band, this variability is consistent with correlated or red noise and is particularly well described by the damped random walk (DRW) model. In this work, we evaluate the feasibility of a new method for identifying spatially unresolved couples of AGN through a fully Bayesian time-domain analysis of the observed light curves (LCs). More specifically, we check whether observed LCs are better described by a single DRW, which we interpret as emitted by a single massive black hole (MBH), or a pair of independent DRWs, generated by a pair of MBHs. We test the method on mock LCs associated with a single MBH and pairs generated with different cadences and lengths of observational campaigns. We constrained the occurrence of false positives, that is, the percentage of single MBH LCs that show substantial evidence in favour of the unresolved MBH pair scenario, finding a fraction of 0.2% and 0.59% in the even and uneven sampling scenarios. We discuss how well the method recovers the model parameters, showing that about 51% and 7% of the simulated LCs have all the recovered parameters within 20% of their true values in our best scenario of evenly sampled LCs for the single MBH and MBH pair scenarios, respectively. We finally study the region of the parameter space in which the detection of an MBH pair is possible, finding that such objects can be correctly identified if the timescales of the process describing the noise are very different, with a ratio smaller than ~0.2, and the variability amplitudes are similar, with their ratio bigger than ~0.2. When limiting to such a region of the parameter space, the fraction of pairs with all the recovered parameters within 20% of the injected values increases up to about 14% and 8% for evenly and unevenly sampled LCs, respectively.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a Bayesian method to identify unresolved AGN pairs by modeling their light curves as single or dual damped random walks, achieving low false positive rates and parameter recovery depending on timescale and amplitude differences, thus enabling detection of massive black hole binaries in specific conditions.
AI.motivation: To develop and evaluate a method for identifying spatially unresolved pairs of active galactic nuclei (AGN) via time-domain analysis of their optical/UV light curves, due to intrinsic variability described by damped random walk (DRW) models.
AI.method: A fully Bayesian analysis comparing whether observed light curves are better modeled by a single DRW (single massive black hole) or two independent DRWs (pair of massive black holes), tested on simulated light curves with varied sampling cadences and observation lengths.
AI.result: The method yields very low false positive rates (0.2%-0.59%) and can recover model parameters within 20% accuracy for about 51% of single black hole and 7% of black hole pair simulations under optimal evenly-sampled conditions. Detection is feasible when timescale ratios are below ~0.2 and variability amplitude ratios exceed ~0.2, increasing parameter recovery rates to 14% (even sampling) and 8% (uneven sampling).
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian time-domain analysis effectively discriminates between single and unresolved pairs of AGN based on optical/UV variability properties in specific parameter regimes, demonstrating a viable approach to identify spatially unresolved massive black hole pairs from their light curves.

title: Generalized Predictions for the Electromagnetic Signatures of Mirror Stars
comment: 13 pages + references, 6 figures. Results made publicly available on https://github.com/davidrcurtin/mirror_star_emissions
summary: Mirror Stars are a generic prediction of dissipative dark matter models, including minimal atomic dark matter and twin baryons in the Mirror Twin Higgs. Mirror Stars capture regular atoms from the interstellar medium through highly suppressed kinetic mixing interactions between the regular and the dark photon. This results in the accumulation of a "nugget", which draws heat from the mirror star core and emits distinctive X-ray and optical signals. In this work, we solve the stellar structure equations of optically thick nuggets across a wide range of the effective mirror star parameter space, and characterize their emission spectra using stellar atmosphere models. This complements an earlier analysis of lower-mass optically thin nuggets. We find that optically thick mirror star nuggets occupy distinct regions of the (stellar surface temperature, luminosity, surface gravity) space, and can be distinguished from regular stars in both HR diagrams and temperature-surface-gravity diagrams using astrometric and spectroscopic stellar catalogues. Our detailed predictions, which are publicly available, now give for the first time a general picture of mirror star signals in the optical and IR to enable realistic mirror star searches using existing catalogues and new telescope observations.

AI.tldr: This work models optically thick mirror star nuggets, revealing distinctive emission patterns that differentiate them from regular stars, and provides predictions to guide their observational detection in optical and IR surveys.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive understanding of mirror star signals by extending previous analyses from optically thin to optically thick nuggets and enable realistic searches for mirror stars in existing and new astronomical data.
AI.method: The study solves stellar structure equations for optically thick mirror star nuggets across a broad parameter space and uses stellar atmosphere models to characterize their emission spectra.
AI.result: Optically thick mirror star nuggets occupy distinct regions in the stellar parameter space, emitting characteristic X-ray and optical signals, and predictions were produced that facilitate the identification of these objects in astrometric and spectroscopic catalogues.
AI.conclusion: Optically thick mirror star nuggets exhibit unique emission characteristics that allow them to be distinguished from regular stars using HR diagrams and temperature-surface-gravity plots in stellar catalogues.

title: Traces of Helium Detected in Type Ic Supernova 2014L
summary: The absence of helium features in optical spectra is one of the classification criteria for Type Ic supernovae (SNe Ic). However, it is highly debated whether helium is truly absent in ejecta or spectroscopically undetectable in the optical region. The near-infrared (NIR) region contains cleaner He lines that are less blended with other common ions in SNe Ic ejecta. We perform full spectral modeling on the near-peak-light optical and NIR spectra of the SN Ic 2014L to quantitatively constrain helium and other outer-ejecta properties, using the radiative transfer code TARDIS. We employ a deep-learning emulator for SNe Ic spectra that serves as a fast surrogate for TARDIS simulations. We then integrate the emulator within the Bayesian inference framework to infer the ejecta properties. The emulator achieves a mean fractional error of 1% between the emulated and TARDIS fluxes across all wavelengths and all samples in the test dataset. We constrain 0.018 to 0.020 M_sun (16% to 84% posterior percentile) of He above the photosphere near peak light in SN 2014L, inferred from the observed spectra covering 3500A to 24000A. A Bayesian statistical test shows that the observed spectra are inconsistent with no helium. Furthermore, the posterior favors a power-law density exponent of -7.04 to -6.88 (16% to 84% credible interval), consistent with theoretical calculations of radiation-dominated explosions. This work demonstrates that Bayesian radiative-transfer inference over a wide wavelength range provides a powerful path toward systematic constraints on He in SNe Ic.

AI.tldr: Using deep-learning accelerated Bayesian spectral modeling of optical and NIR data, helium was quantitatively detected in SN Ic 2014L ejecta, resolving debates over helium absence in Type Ic supernovae and confirming a density structure consistent with theoretical explosion models.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debate on whether helium is truly absent or just spectroscopically undetectable in optical spectra of Type Ic supernovae ejecta by using near-infrared data with cleaner He lines.
AI.method: Full spectral modeling of near-peak-light optical and near-infrared spectra of SN Ic 2014L using the radiative transfer code TARDIS, accelerated by a deep-learning emulator integrated with a Bayesian inference framework to quantitatively infer ejecta properties.
AI.result: Detected 0.018 to 0.020 solar masses of helium above the photosphere near peak light in SN 2014L from 3500Å to 24000Å spectra; Bayesian analysis rejects the no-helium hypothesis and finds a power-law density exponent consistent with radiation-dominated explosion models.
AI.conclusion: Helium is present in the ejecta of SN Ic 2014L and can be systematically constrained through Bayesian radiative-transfer modeling over a broad wavelength range, demonstrating that helium is not absent but spectroscopically detectable using near-infrared spectra.

title: Non-Cold Dark Matter from Memory-Burdened Primordial Black Holes
summary: Non-cold dark matter particles can arise from the evaporation of primordial black holes (PBHs). In this paper, we further investigate how the memory-burden effect, which delays the full evaporation of black holes, affects the Lyman-$α$ bound on such non-cold dark matter (NCDM) particles. We mainly focus on scenarios in which PBHs have fully evaporated by today, undergoing a semi-classical evaporation phase followed by a memory-burden dominated phase. In this framework, PBH evaporation generically leads to two distinct dark-matter populations with different velocity dispersions, which can imprint observable signatures on the matter power spectrum. We compute the resulting NCDM phase-space distribution and its impact on small-scale overdensities using the $\texttt{BlackHawk}$ and $\texttt{CLASS}$ codes. This is then used to reinterpret Lyman-$α$ forest constraints for thermal warm dark matter, deriving both a velocity-dispersion-based and a matter-power-spectrum-based estimate. In particular, we discuss how we obtain constraints on scenarios in which NCDM particles constitute only a fraction of the total relic dark matter. Finally, we discuss the viable parameter space as a function of dark matter masses, PBH initial conditions, and memory-burden parameters. We show that even subdominant NCDM components from PBH evaporation can be constrained, and confirm that NCDM can only account for all of the dark matter in the absence of PBH domination, as in the semi-classical case.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how the memory-burden effect during primordial black hole evaporation influences the properties and observational constraints of non-cold dark matter particles produced in this process, using detailed modeling and simulations to reinterpret Lyman-alpha forest bounds and define constraints on dark matter and PBH parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate how the memory-burden effect, which delays full evaporation of primordial black holes, impacts constraints on non-cold dark matter produced by PBH evaporation, particularly regarding Lyman-alpha bounds.
AI.method: Modeling PBH evaporation including a semi-classical phase and memory-burden dominated phase, computing resulting non-cold dark matter phase-space distributions and velocity dispersions using BlackHawk and CLASS codes, then reinterpreting Lyman-alpha forest constraints on thermal warm dark matter to estimate bounds on NCDM from PBHs.
AI.result: Identified two distinct dark matter populations with different velocity dispersions from PBH evaporation; constrained scenarios where NCDM constitutes only a fraction of dark matter; showed NCDM can constitute all dark matter only without PBH domination; defined viable parameter space as function of dark matter mass, PBH initial conditions, and memory-burden parameters.
AI.conclusion: The memory-burden effect significantly alters constraints on PBH-evaporated non-cold dark matter, yielding observable signatures in matter power spectra and tightening Lyman-alpha bounds even for subdominant NCDM fractions, while confirming full NCDM dark matter scenarios require no PBH domination.

title: A Novel Method to Construct Frequency-Domain Gravitational Waveform for Accelerating Sources
summary: Accurately modeling the inspiral-merger-ringdown (IMR) signal of coalescing compact objects is essential for the test of general relativity. However, it is known that astrophysical environments can distort gravitational-wave (GW) signal and, if ignored, may bias parameter estimation or even our understanding of gravity. Previous studies suggest that various astrophysical environmental effects can be modeled in a unified way by introducing an effective acceleration. However, such models are based on stationary phase approximation (SPA) and post-Newtonian (PN) formalism, which are inconsistent with the fast orbital evolution and strong gravity in the final merger-ringdown phase. To overcome this limit, we introduce frequency-domain spectral differentiation (FSD), which maps the time shift of the signal caused by acceleration into a differentiation in the frequency domain. The mapping does not rely on SPA or PN formalism, therefore can be used to construct the accelerated waveform across the entire IMR phases. We compare the FSD waveforms with the conventional SPA+PN ones, and find that the former more faithfully match the simulated signals of accelerating sources, especially in the merger-ringdown phase and when higher-order FSD corrections are included. A Fisher information matrix analysis suggests that FSD waveforms can achieve higher precision than SPA+PN waveforms in measuring effective acceleration. Therefore, the FSD method offers a more self-consistent treatment of various astrophysical environmental effects in the final merger-ringdown phase of binary GW sources.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a frequency-domain spectral differentiation method to model gravitational-wave signals under acceleration, overcoming limitations of previous approaches and improving accuracy in the critical merger-ringdown phase for better parameter estimation and tests of gravity.
AI.motivation: Previous models of astrophysical environmental effects on gravitational waves rely on SPA and PN approximations that fail to accurately capture fast orbital evolution and strong gravity near merger, potentially biasing parameter estimation and tests of general relativity.
AI.method: Developed the FSD technique which maps time shifts caused by effective acceleration into differentiations in the frequency domain, bypassing the limitations of the stationary phase approximation and post-Newtonian formalism and enabling waveform construction over the entire inspiral-merger-ringdown phases.
AI.result: FSD waveforms more faithfully match simulated signals of accelerating sources, particularly in the merger-ringdown phase and with higher-order corrections, and a Fisher information matrix analysis shows improved precision in measuring effective acceleration compared to SPA+PN waveforms.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-domain spectral differentiation (FSD) method provides a more accurate and consistent modeling of gravitational-wave signals from coalescing compact objects under acceleration, especially in the merger-ringdown phase, compared to previous SPA+PN based models.

title: Lagrangian Bias as a Gaussian Random Field
summary: Halo bias is typically treated as a set of coefficients in a perturbative expansion. We show instead that every point in a Gaussian density field has a well-defined scale-independent Lagrangian bias, thereby defining a bias field. This property can be extended to any linear operator acting on the Lagrangian density field, generating secondary bias fields. Halo bias then arises from geometric selection of Lagrangian patches within this pre-existing field, rather than being generated by collapse. We demonstrate that this framework predicts the measured $b(M)$ relation for halos. The multivariate Gaussian structure of the fields naturally explains the Gaussian distribution of halo bias at fixed mass and assembly bias. The results presented here motivate combining this framework with a forward model of halo collapse, yielding an ab initio model for halo clustering.

AI.tldr: This work shows that halo bias can be understood as scale-independent Lagrangian bias fields in Gaussian initial conditions, predicting halo clustering properties and motivating models combining this with halo collapse dynamics.
AI.motivation: To reconceptualize halo bias not as perturbative coefficients but as intrinsic bias fields within Gaussian initial density conditions, enabling a more fundamental understanding of halo clustering.
AI.method: Analyzing Gaussian density fields to define scale-independent Lagrangian bias at each point, extending this to secondary bias fields via linear operators, and comparing predicted halo bias with measurements to validate the framework.
AI.result: The approach reproduces the measured halo bias-mass relation and explains the Gaussian distribution of halo bias and assembly bias, supporting the idea that halo bias arises from geometric selection in the initial density field.
AI.conclusion: Halo bias originates from the geometric selection of Lagrangian patches within a pre-existing Gaussian Lagrangian bias field rather than from halo collapse, providing a predictive framework consistent with observed mass-dependent bias relations and assembly bias.

title: A large misalignment between continuous jet and discrete ejecta in microquasar GRS 1915+105 during its obscured phase
summary: We report a large misalignment between the continuous jet and the discrete ejecta in GRS 1915+105, detected in April 2023 with the East Asian VLBI network (EAVN). Two-sided ejecta are shown at 6.7 GHz images and central continuous jets are resolved at 43 GHz by EAVN quasi-simultaneously. While the continuous jet was aligned with the long-standing jet position angle (PA) of about 147 degree, the discrete ejecta appeared at a markedly different PA about 188 degree, with the lowest intrinsic velocity about 0.35 c ever reported. A similar misalignment of PA between discrete ejecta and continuous jet was independently detected in late September of 2023 during a consecutive flare event. The pronounced and recurrent angular deviations suggest a time-variable jet launching geometry, which, in conjunction with the observed X-ray obscuration, can be attributable to a warped accretion disk. Our result could offer new insight into the fundamental differences between continuous jet and discrete ejecta, and broadly provides a clue to understand the phenomena for transient black hole X-Ray binaries and changing-look active galactic nuclei during the X-ray obscured phase.

AI.tldr: This study reveals a pronounced, recurrent misalignment between continuous jets and discrete ejecta in GRS 1915+105, attributed to a warped, dynamically changing accretion disk, enhancing our understanding of jet launching and behavior in black hole systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental differences and dynamic behaviors between continuous jets and discrete ejecta in black hole X-ray binaries, particularly addressing observed misalignments and their physical origins.
AI.method: High-resolution VLBI observations using the East Asian VLBI network (EAVN) at 6.7 GHz and 43 GHz frequencies to image both the two-sided discrete ejecta and the resolved continuous jet quasi-simultaneously in GRS 1915+105.
AI.result: Detection of a significant and recurrent misalignment between the position angles of the continuous jet (about 147°) and the discrete ejecta (about 188°) with the ejecta's intrinsic velocity being as low as 0.35 c; evidence suggesting a time-variable jet launching geometry aligned with a warped accretion disk, corroborated by associated X-ray obscuration events.
AI.conclusion: The observed persistent angular deviations between continuous jets and discrete ejecta indicate a warped, time-variable jet launching mechanism in GRS 1915+105, offering new insights into jet formation processes and aiding the understanding of jet behaviors in transient black hole X-ray binaries and changing-look active galactic nuclei during their X-ray obscured phases.

title: Eppur non si trovano Vol. 2: No Planetary-mass Primordial Black Holes toward the Andromeda Galaxy
comment: submitted to Acta Astronomica, comments on arXiv:2602.05840
summary: A recent preprint by Sugiyama et al. reported the discovery of twelve candidates for short-timescale (less than one day) gravitational microlensing events based on high-cadence photometric observations of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) using the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam. These detections were attributed to a large population of planetary-mass primordial black holes (PBHs) that could account for the entirety of the dark matter in the Milky Way and M31 halos. However, these results are in clear tension with previous searches for short-timescale microlensing events toward the Magellanic Clouds, such as those by the OGLE survey. In addition, both the temporal and spatial distributions of the Subaru candidates are inconsistent with expectations for microlensing events. Here, we reanalyze the Subaru data using an independent difference image analysis photometric pipeline. We find that all twelve candidates identified by Sugiyama et al. exhibit asymmetric light curves and/or variability on multiple nights of Subaru observations. Our analysis reveals that among them ten objects are RR Lyrae stars, one is an eclipsing binary, and one is an unclassified variable star. We find no compelling evidence for short-timescale microlensing events among the candidates identified in the Subaru data set, nor for a significant population of planetary-mass PBHs as dark matter components. Our results underscore the necessity of robust variable-star rejection in high-cadence microlensing searches using large telescopes.

AI.tldr: A reanalysis of Subaru data disproves previous claims of short-timescale microlensing events caused by planetary-mass primordial black holes; the candidates are variable stars, not microlensing, emphasizing careful variable-star filtering.
AI.motivation: To verify the claimed detection of short-timescale gravitational microlensing events in M31 suggesting planetary-mass primordial black holes as dark matter, which conflicts with prior studies and expected microlensing distributions.
AI.method: Reanalysis of Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam data using an independent difference image analysis photometric pipeline to examine the nature of the twelve candidate events identified by Sugiyama et al.
AI.result: All twelve candidates exhibited asymmetric light curves or multi-night variability; ten were identified as RR Lyrae stars, one as an eclipsing binary, and one as an unclassified variable star, with no convincing microlensing events found.
AI.conclusion: There is no compelling evidence for short-timescale microlensing events or a significant population of planetary-mass primordial black holes as dark matter in the Subaru data, highlighting the need for rigorous variable-star rejection in such searches.

title: A Universal 1.5 GeV Gamma-Ray Line in Active Galactic Nuclei
summary: We report the detection of a gamma-ray spectral line at approximately 1.5 GeV in three active galactic nuclei (AGN) using 17 years of Fermi-LAT observations. The sample includes both blazars (with relativistic jets directed toward Earth) and a radio galaxy (with a misaligned jet, free from significant beaming effects). The line is detected with local significances of $\sim$4.1$σ$, $\sim$3.9$σ$, and $\sim$2.8$σ$ in the individual sources. A joint likelihood analysis yields a combined test statistic TS $\simeq$ 57.77, corresponding to a significance well above 5$σ$. The line flux remains stable over the full observation period, in contrast to the variable continuum emission from the AGN. The appearance of an identical spectral feature in astrophysically distinct environments is difficult to reconcile with standard jet-based emission mechanisms. While a conventional astrophysical explanation remains elusive, the signal's characteristics are consistent with predictions for dark matter annihilation. This finding motivates further investigation into the nature of this spectral feature and its possible connection to particle dark matter.

AI.tldr: A stable 1.5 GeV gamma-ray line was detected in three AGN over 17 years of Fermi-LAT data, inconsistent with typical jet emissions but consistent with dark matter annihilation signatures, prompting further study.
AI.motivation: To identify and understand the nature of a persistent gamma-ray spectral line feature observed in different types of active galactic nuclei (AGN), potentially linked to fundamental physics beyond standard astrophysical processes.
AI.method: Analyzed 17 years of Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations from three AGN, including both blazars and a radio galaxy, using individual significance calculations and a joint likelihood analysis to detect and confirm the spectral line.
AI.result: Detected a stable gamma-ray spectral line at about 1.5 GeV across three distinct AGN with combined significance greater than 5σ, showing consistency over time despite variable continuum emission. The feature challenges conventional jet emission models and aligns with theoretical predictions for dark matter annihilation.
AI.conclusion: The detection of an identical, stable 1.5 GeV gamma-ray line in multiple AGN types suggests a phenomenon not easily explained by standard astrophysical jet emissions, supporting the hypothesis of a dark matter-related origin and warranting further investigation into this spectral feature.

title: Calibrating optical galaxy cluster projection effects with sparse spectroscopic samples: A clustering redshift approach
summary: Wide-field optical imaging surveys are efficient at identifying galaxy clusters, but optically identified clusters suffer from projection effects--physically unassociated galaxies along the line of sight can be misidentified as cluster members due to distance uncertainties. Previous studies have used spectroscopic follow-up observations of cluster members to quantify projection effects; however, such follow-up efforts cannot keep pace with the rapidly growing cluster samples. On the other hand, spectroscopic surveys designed for large-scale structure studies collect tens of millions of spectra but tend to have sparse spectra in cluster regions. To bridge this gap, we develop a clustering redshift approach that cross-correlates cluster members with sparse, non-cluster-targeted spectroscopic galaxy samples. We validate this approach using the Cardinal simulation, recovering the correct spectroscopic distribution and projection effect parameters of redMaPPer cluster members. Our approach is insensitive to the selection of the spectroscopic sample and paves the way for calibrating the upcoming LSST clusters using DESI and Roman spectroscopic samples.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a clustering redshift method to correct projection effects in optically identified galaxy clusters by cross-correlating with sparse spectroscopic samples, validated via simulation, paving the way for calibrating large cluster surveys with upcoming spectroscopic data.
AI.motivation: Optically identified galaxy clusters suffer from projection effects due to distance uncertainties, complicating accurate cluster member identification, and existing spectroscopic follow-ups cannot scale with growing cluster samples.
AI.method: Developed a clustering redshift method that cross-correlates optical cluster members with sparse, non-cluster-targeted spectroscopic galaxy samples to quantify projection effects.
AI.result: Validated the method using Cardinal simulation, successfully recovering correct spectroscopic distributions and projection effect parameters of cluster members, and demonstrated method's insensitivity to spectroscopic sample selection.
AI.conclusion: The clustering redshift approach effectively calibrates projection effects in optically identified galaxy clusters, enabling scalable use of large spectroscopic surveys for upcoming wide-field imaging cluster surveys like LSST with DESI and Roman data.

title: 20 years of monitoring: PKS 2155-304 and PKS 1510-089 in the eyes of Swift and Fermi. I. The case of PKS 2155-304
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures; resubmitted to JHEAp after first referee round
summary: We present a comprehensive 20-year multiwavelength variability study of the blazar PKS 2155-304, one of the most luminous and extensively monitored high-frequency-peaked BL Lac objects in the southern hemisphere. Using Fermi-LAT $γ$-ray data together with Swift-XRT and UVOT observations spanning 2005-2024, we trace the long-term evolution of its flux, interband correlations, and spectral behaviour across the optical, X-ray, and $γ$-ray bands. All flux distributions are compatible with log-normality. Interestingly, the optical domain exhibited a notable baseline change around 2009, but this has no strong influence on the fit of the flux distribution. While interband flux-flux correlations are found, no stable temporal lags emerge. This implies varying correlation patterns between epochs. The X-ray emission displays a robust harder-when-brighter trend, however with epoch-dependent slopes, while the $γ$-ray spectra show only mild flux dependence. The fractional variability increases systematically with energy within a given radiation component. No direct correlation of the year-wise fractional variability with the corresponding average flux could be found. Interestingly, a pronounced X-ray spectral upturn, detected during a low state in 2012, points to an additional radiative component. As the connection from this upturn to the $γ$-ray spectrum is not smooth, it probably is not the onset of the inverse-Compton component, but more likely points either to a hadronic contribution or an additional spatially-separate emission zone. These findings reveal the complexity of variability patterns in PKS 2155-304 and the non-uniform nature of its particle acceleration and emission processes.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive 20-year study of PKS 2155-304 reveals complex multiwavelength variability with log-normal flux distributions, energy-dependent fractional variability, and evidence for additional emission components beyond traditional models.
AI.motivation: To understand the long-term multiwavelength variability and emission processes of the blazar PKS 2155-304, a highly luminous and well-monitored high-frequency-peaked BL Lac object.
AI.method: A 20-year multiwavelength variability study analyzing Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data alongside Swift-XRT and UVOT observations from 2005 to 2024, investigating flux distributions, interband correlations, spectral behavior, and variability trends across optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands.
AI.result: Flux distributions are log-normal; optical baseline changed around 2009 without affecting flux distribution fits; interband correlations exist but with variable temporal lags; X-ray emission shows a harder-when-brighter trend with variable slopes; gamma-ray spectral flux dependence is mild; fractional variability increases with energy; a pronounced X-ray spectral upturn during a 2012 low state suggests a secondary radiative component distinct from inverse-Compton emission, possibly hadronic or from a separate emission zone.
AI.conclusion: PKS 2155-304 exhibits complex, non-uniform variability and emission patterns, indicating diverse particle acceleration and radiative processes, challenging simple emission models and suggesting contributions from multiple components or zones.

title: Relic Magnetic Fields from Non-Adiabatic Photon Freeze-Out at Recombination
summary:
We propose a new mechanism for generating a primordial electromagnetic relic during the recombination--decoupling transition, based on the rate-dependent thermodynamics of the cosmic photon gas. Treating the photon sector as an open system coupled to the electron plasma, we show that a finite Thomson relaxation rate generates a departure from instantaneous thermal equilibrium, leading to non-adiabatic mode squeezing. As this relaxation rate rapidly decreases across recombination, the system quickly loses the ability to further amplify the deviation, and the squeezing freezes out at a small but finite value. This dynamics is naturally described as a narrow transition layer between an adiabatic tracking regime and a post-relaxation freeze-out regime. By a canonical transformation, the reduced evolution equation is recast into a forced oscillator with a smooth effective potential, clarifying the origin of the squeezing and the selection of the relic scale.
  Projecting the resulting non-equilibrium electromagnetic relic onto the magnetic sector, we derive the corresponding spectrum and show that its characteristic peak is controlled not by the squeezing parameter alone but by the weighted combination \(k^3\mathscr S_k\). In representative realizations, the peak corresponds today to scales of order \(10\)--\(20\) Mpc, while the present-day field amplitude remains extremely small. The mechanism is therefore better viewed as a source of a frozen non-equilibrium electromagnetic relic than as a complete explanation of the observed cosmic magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new thermodynamic mechanism for primordial electromagnetic relic generation during recombination, involving finite Thomson relaxation-induced mode squeezing, resulting in a frozen relic spectrum peaked at ~10-20 Mpc scales but with very small amplitude, insufficient alone to explain cosmic magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: To explain the generation of primordial electromagnetic relics during the cosmic recombination--decoupling transition through a thermodynamic mechanism involving the photon gas and electron plasma interaction.
AI.method: Modeling the photon sector as an open system coupled with electron plasma, incorporating the finite Thomson relaxation rate, and employing a canonical transformation to recast the evolution equation into a forced oscillator framework with a smooth effective potential.
AI.result: Identification of a non-adiabatic mode squeezing effect caused by the relaxation rate dynamics, leading to a frozen electromagnetic relic spectrum with a characteristic peak at 10-20 Mpc scales today, but with extremely small present-day field amplitude, indicating the mechanism alone does not fully explain observed cosmic magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism generates a non-equilibrium primordial electromagnetic relic during recombination via rate-dependent thermodynamics and mode squeezing, producing a scale-specific relic spectrum; however, its amplitude is too small to account for observed cosmic magnetic fields, serving better as a source of frozen non-equilibrium relic rather than a complete explanation.

title: 20 years of monitoring: PKS 2155-304 and PKS 1510-089 in the eyes of Swift and Fermi. II. PKS 1510-089 and comparison
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, resubmitted to JHEAp after first referee round
summary: We present a comprehensive, two-decade, multiwavelength variability study of the blazar PKS 1510-089, one of the most prominent and extensively monitored flat-spectrum radio quasars. Using Fermi-LAT $γ$-ray data together with Swift-XRT and UVOT observations spanning 2005-2024, we trace the long-term evolution of its flux, interband correlations, and spectral behaviour across the optical, X-ray, and $γ$-ray bands. We find that the HE $γ$-ray and X-ray flux distributions are log-normal, while the optical distributions are compatible with double-log-normal functions. The latter may be due to contributions from the accretion disk. The range of fluxes in a given band, as well as the fractional variability values are in-line with the expectations that high-energy parts of a given spectral component are more variable than low-energy parts. No obvious cross-correlations exist between the bands over the 20 years of observations. The X-ray and $γ$-ray spectra are variable, but do not show any trend with flux. These results are suggestive of different zones being active in the jet of PKS 1510-089 at any given time. In a previous paper, we used the same techniques to study the high-frequency-peaked BL Lac object PKS 2155-304. Both sources follow the aforementioned trend on the energy-dependent variability of the spectral components, as well as the lack of significant cross-correlations between the studied bands. While PKS 2155-304 exhibits a harder-when-brighter behaviour in its high-energy part of the synchrotron component, no such behaviour could be found in PKS 1510-089. Both sources show orphan flares, which can seemingly happen in any band. In summary, the long-term studies of these two sources reveal that the underlying physics is similar in these apparently different source classes, even though variability patterns keep changing and remain unpredictable.

AI.tldr: A 20-year multiwavelength study of blazar PKS 1510-089 reveals log-normal flux distributions, energy-dependent variability, no cross-band correlations, and spectral variability without flux trends, paralleling behaviors in another blazar, suggesting similar underlying jet physics across blazar types despite unpredictable variability.
AI.motivation: To understand the long-term multiwavelength variability behavior of the blazar PKS 1510-089 and compare it with another blazar, aiming to reveal insights about the jet emission and variability mechanisms.
AI.method: A two-decade study utilizing Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data combined with Swift-XRT and UVOT optical and X-ray observations from 2005 to 2024; analysis included flux distribution fitting, interband correlation checks, and spectral variability studies across optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands.
AI.result: HE gamma-ray and X-ray flux distributions are log-normal; optical flux distributions fit double-log-normal models likely due to accretion disk contributions. The variability amplitude follows the energy-dependent trend with higher variability at higher energies in spectral components. No significant cross-band correlations over 20 years were found. The spectra vary but without flux-dependent trends. Both studied sources share similar underlying physics despite different source classifications and unpredictable variability patterns.
AI.conclusion: The variability patterns in PKS 1510-089 suggest multiple active emission zones in the jet without clear cross-band correlations, similar to findings in PKS 2155-304. The physics governing variability appear to be consistent across different blazar types, even though variability remains complex and unpredictable.

title: A Geometric Theory of Cosmological Structure via Entropic Curvature in Wasserstein Space
summary: We construct a geometric framework for cosmological large-scale structure based on optimal transport theory and Wasserstein geometry. In this framework, Ricci curvature on the probability measure space $\mathcal{P}_2(M)$ is characterized by the geodesic convexity of entropy and is formulated as the response of probability distributions to optimal transport. We introduce effective Ricci curvatures $K_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(\infty)}$ and $K_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(N)}$ associated with Kullback--Leibler-type and Rényi-type entropies, corresponding respectively to the curvature-dimension conditions CD$(K,\infty)$ and CD$(K,N)$. By localizing these curvatures to finite scales using local and reference measures, we construct curvature indicators applicable to observational data. Under a local quadratic approximation, the effective curvature reduces to the Hessian of the log-density, showing that conventional Hessian-based structure classifications arise as a limiting case of the present framework. We further show that effective curvature depends on observational scale and formulate this dependence as a scale flow, distinct from Ricci flow because it describes a change of resolution rather than a time evolution of geometry. Treating curvature as a random field then extends the statistical description of density fields: curvature statistics are given by higher-order weighted integrals of the power spectrum and by spatial derivatives of the correlation function, emphasizing geometric rather than amplitude information. This framework provides a unified connection between optimal transport geometry and cosmological structure analysis, and offers a new perspective on multiscale structure and nonlinear statistics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric framework based on optimal transport and Wasserstein geometry to analyze large-scale cosmological structures via effective Ricci curvatures, linking entropy convexity to curvature, introducing scale-dependent curvature measures, and extending statistical descriptions, thereby unifying and advancing multiscale cosmological structure analysis.
AI.motivation: To develop a geometric framework for analyzing cosmological large-scale structure rooted in optimal transport theory and Wasserstein geometry, enabling a novel characterization of Ricci curvature on probability measures relevant to cosmology.
AI.method: Constructing Ricci curvature on the space of probability measures via geodesic convexity of entropy; introducing effective Ricci curvatures linked to Kullback--Leibler and Rényi entropies under curvature-dimension conditions CD(K,∞) and CD(K,N); localizing curvatures to finite scales via local and reference measures; approximating curvature with the Hessian of log-density; formulating scale dependence as a scale flow; treating curvature as a random field to relate curvature statistics to power spectrum integrals and correlation function derivatives.
AI.result: Established effective Ricci curvatures as scale-dependent geometrical indicators for cosmological data, showed conventional Hessian-based classifications emerge as limiting cases, formulated a novel scale flow distinct from Ricci flow describing resolution changes, and linked curvature statistics to higher-order spectral measures, thus providing a unified geometric-statistical framework connecting optimal transport and cosmological structure analysis.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a new geometric approach integrating optimal transport and Wasserstein geometry to quantify cosmological structures through effective Ricci curvature measures. This framework unifies previous Hessian-based classifications, explicates scale-dependent structural features via scale flow, and enhances statistical analysis of density fields with curvature statistics, offering profound insights into multiscale and nonlinear characteristics of large-scale cosmic structures.

title: Resolving Oblique Star-Disk Collisions in Quasi-Periodic Eruptions: Numerical Requirements and the Importance of Geometry
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, and 1 table. Submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Star-disk collisions have been proposed as a promising mechanism for producing quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) in galactic nuclei. Because the stellar atmospheric scale height is orders of magnitude smaller than the stellar radius, studying the shock launching by stars poses a significant numerical challenge. We implement an immersed solid-boundary method in Athena++ to study bow-shock formation and ejecta launching when a solid sphere crosses an accretion disk at supersonic speed. After validating the method against experimental results for solid bodies in uniform flows, we perform two- and three-dimensional adiabatic simulations of star-disk collisions. We find that resolving the bow-shock stand-off distance during the compression phase is essential: under-resolved simulations severely underestimate the ejecta mass and energy. When adequately resolved, the ejecta properties agree well with analytical estimates. We further show that collision geometry plays a critical role. Oblique encounters, which arise naturally due to disk rotation, allow easier shock breakout from the disk's backside and substantially reduce the luminosity contrast between forward and backward ejecta compared to perpendicular collisions. These results emphasize the importance of both numerical resolution and three-dimensional geometry in modeling star-disk collisions and interpreting QPEs.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a high-resolution 3D simulation method to study shock and ejecta formation during star-disk collisions, showing that proper resolution and collision angle critically impact ejecta properties and are vital for understanding quasi-periodic eruptions in galactic nuclei.
AI.motivation: To address the numerical challenges in accurately modeling shock launching by stars during star-disk collisions, which are proposed as mechanisms for quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) in galactic nuclei.
AI.method: Implemented an immersed solid-boundary method in Athena++ to simulate bow-shock formation and ejecta launching when a solid sphere crosses an accretion disk at supersonic speed; conducted validation against experiments and performed 2D and 3D adiabatic simulations.
AI.result: Found that resolving the bow-shock stand-off distance is crucial for correct ejecta mass and energy estimation; ejecta properties match analytical predictions when well-resolved; collision geometry significantly affects shock breakout and luminosity contrasts between forward and backward ejecta, with oblique collisions facilitating easier shock breakout and lower luminosity contrasts.
AI.conclusion: High numerical resolution and 3D geometric modeling are essential to accurately simulate star-disk collisions and interpret QPE observations; oblique collision geometries inherent to disk rotation critically influence ejecta dynamics and luminosity patterns.

title: Euclid preparation. Impact of redshift distribution uncertainties on the joint analysis of photometric galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing
summary: One of the $\textit{Euclid}$ mission's key projects is the so-called 3$\times$2pt analysis, that is, the combination of cosmic shear, photometric galaxy clustering, and galaxy-galaxy lensing. Although $\textit{Euclid}$ has established quality requirements for the photo-$z$ accuracy needed for the weak lensing galaxy sample, no such requirements have been set for the photometric clustering sample. In this paper, we investigate the impact of redshift uncertainties on $\textit{Euclid}$'s photometric galaxy clustering analysis and its combination with weak gravitational lensing, focusing on data release 1 (DR1). In particular, we study whether having precise knowledge of the mean of the redshift distributions per bin is sufficient to avoid biases in the resulting cosmological constraints or whether accuracy in the higher-order moments of the distribution is required. We evaluate the results based on their constraining power on $w_{\mathrm{0}}$ and $w_{a}$ and define thresholds for the precision and accuracy of $\textit{Euclid}$'s redshift distribution of the photometric clustering sample. We find that the redshift distributions of the photometric clustering sample must be known at an accuracy of 0.004(1+$z$) in the mean in order to recover 80$\%$ of the constraining power in $\textit{Euclid}$'s DR1 $w_{\mathrm{0}}w_{a}$CDM 3$\times$2pt analysis. The impact of the uncertainty on the width is negligible, provided the mean redshift is constrained with sufficient accuracy. For most sources of redshift distribution error, attaining the requirement on the mean will also reduce uncertainty in the width well below the required level.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for Euclid's photometric clustering analysis combined with weak lensing, accurate mean redshift knowledge (0.004(1+z)) is crucial for robust dark energy parameter constraints, while errors in distribution width have minimal impact.
AI.motivation: To determine the impact of redshift uncertainties on Euclid's photometric galaxy clustering analysis and its combination with weak gravitational lensing, focusing on improving cosmological constraints.
AI.method: Analyzing the effect of redshift distribution uncertainties, especially the mean and higher-order moments, on the 3x2pt analysis using Euclid's data release 1, evaluating constraining power on dark energy parameters (w_0, w_a).
AI.result: Found that the mean redshift of photometric clustering samples must be known to an accuracy of 0.004(1+z) to retain 80% of the constraining power on dark energy parameters; uncertainty in distribution width is negligible if the mean is well constrained.
AI.conclusion: Precise knowledge of the mean redshift per bin for photometric clustering samples is essential for unbiased cosmological constraints in Euclid's 3x2pt analysis, whereas accuracy on higher-order moments is less critical.

title: Transport-Geometric Formulation of Peak Statistics: Curvature-Conditioned Point Processes and Response Hierarchy
summary: We develop a geometric formulation of peak statistics in cosmological density fields based on optimal transport and entropy. In this framework, the density field is treated as a probability measure, and its local structure is characterized by the Hessian of the log-density, which arises as the local response of an entropy functional in Wasserstein space. Peaks are thereby defined as positive-curvature stationary points, and their number density is expressed as a curvature-conditioned point process. In the linear Gaussian limit, the joint distribution of local variables closes in terms of a finite set of spectral moments, recovering the standard theory of peak statistics, known as BBKS. This clarifies that BBKS corresponds to a solvable limit of a more general structure combining probability distributions, curvature constraints, and geometric measure. The framework extends naturally beyond Gaussianity and linearity. Deviations from Gaussianity are incorporated as deformations of the joint distribution of curvature variables, while nonlinear structures are described through the curvature of the log-density. We further derive the two- and three-point peak statistics as curvature-conditioned $n$-point measures, and show that the full hierarchy of peak statistics can be organized as response functions to long-wavelength background modes. In this formulation, the conventional peak bias appears as the lowest-order response coefficient, with higher-order correlations arising as its natural extensions. This work embeds peak theory into a unified geometric framework and provides a systematic basis for incorporating nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity, and higher-order statistics, with direct relevance for observational applications.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a geometric framework for cosmological peak statistics using optimal transport and entropy concepts, extending the classical BBKS Gaussian theory to include nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and higher-order statistics, thereby unifying and generalizing peak theory for improved cosmological data analysis.
AI.motivation: To develop a comprehensive and geometrically grounded framework for peak statistics in cosmological density fields that goes beyond the classical Gaussian and linear assumptions of BBKS, allowing for the inclusion of nonlinearities, non-Gaussianities, and higher-order correlations relevant for observational cosmology.
AI.method: The paper formulates peak statistics by treating the density field as a probability measure and characterizing its local structure using the Hessian of the log-density via optimal transport and entropy in Wasserstein space. It expresses peak counts through curvature-conditioned point processes, derives joint distributions using spectral moments in the Gaussian limit, and extends analysis to non-Gaussian and nonlinear regimes through curvature deformations and log-density curvature. Two- and three-point functions and higher-order statistics are framed as response functions to background modes.
AI.result: The authors recover the classical BBKS peak theory as a solvable limit within their framework and provide new expressions for two- and three-point peak statistics and a hierarchy of higher-order statistics interpreted as response functions. They establish that conventional peak bias is the leading-order response, with natural extensions to higher-order correlations, thus offering a systematic and unified geometric approach applicable to a broad range of cosmological conditions.
AI.conclusion: This work successfully embeds peak statistics of cosmological density fields into a unified geometric framework, generalizing the traditional BBKS peak theory and enabling systematic incorporation of nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity, and higher-order statistics.

title: Delayed Radio Flares in Neutrino-associated Blazars: The Case of TXS 0506+056
summary: Radio flares have been postulated to be associated with the production of astrophysical neutrinos. For example, TXS 0506+056 exhibits a 2-3 yr delay between the 2017 IceCube-170922A/$γ$-ray flare and a GHz radio maximum. We quantitatively test if the delayed radio flare originates from the same compact region where neutrinos and $γ$-rays are produced as it expands downstream and synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) is reduced. Starting from the 2017 flare blob parameters, we model the expanding production region and its evolving radio emission with LeHaMoC in a fully time-dependent framework, and compare our 1.2-22 GHz light curves to RATAN-600 data. We study different scenarios with increasing levels of sophistication, including continuous injection and energy re-dissipation on pc scales. While a simple expanding blob scenario fails to reproduce the radio data, a downstream dissipation episode of particles in the optically thin regime, followed by jet deceleration, successfully describes the radio evolution. Within our one-zone time-dependent framework, the delayed radio flare is unlikely to come from an expanding neutrino production zone becoming transparent to radio emission. Additional ingredients are needed, such as re-dissipation downstream with a subsequent Doppler-factor decline. The radio flare is powered by leptonic synchrotron emission and is largely insensitive to the proton population relevant for neutrino production, implying that the delayed radio flare mainly probes downstream dissipation and beaming in certain jet configurations rather than being a genuine feature associated with the neutrino production.

AI.tldr: This study models the delayed radio flare in TXS 0506+056, finding it does not originate from the neutrino production region but from downstream jet processes involving particle re-dissipation and jet deceleration, implying radio flares mainly trace jet dynamics rather than neutrino emission.
AI.motivation: To test if the delayed radio flare observed in TXS 0506+056 originates from the same compact region responsible for neutrino and gamma-ray production and to understand the connection between radio flares and neutrino emissions.
AI.method: Modeled the expanding production region and its evolving radio emission using the LeHaMoC time-dependent framework, starting from 2017 flare blob parameters, and compared the resulting 1.2-22 GHz light curves to RATAN-600 observational data. Various scenarios were tested, including continuous particle injection, energy re-dissipation on parsec scales, and jet deceleration.
AI.result: The simple expanding blob model failed to reproduce radio data, while a scenario involving downstream particle re-dissipation in an optically thin regime and jet deceleration successfully described the radio evolution. The delayed radio flare is unlikely to originate from the neutrino production zone becoming radio transparent. Instead, it is powered by leptonic synchrotron emission and insensitive to the proton population relevant for neutrino production.
AI.conclusion: The delayed radio flare in TXS 0506+056 does not directly trace neutrino production but instead probes downstream jet dissipation and relativistic beaming effects. Additional physical processes beyond simple expansion, such as downstream particle re-acceleration and Doppler factor changes, are necessary to explain the radio observations.

title: Universal Non-Gaussian Signatures from Transient Instabilities
summary: We identify universal signatures in the bispectrum arising from a transient tachyonic instability of entropic fluctuations during inflation, a phenomenon that naturally arises in hyperbolic field-space geometries. We perform exact numerical calculations directly at the level of fluctuations, without relying on a specific background model, and distinguish two cases. In the light case, with masses around the Hubble scale, our results provide the first-ever computation of the bispectrum due to such tachyonic instabilities. We find a universal magnification of the folded configuration, together with the known non-analytic scaling in the squeezed limit. As an illustrative example, we compute and analyse the bispectrum in angular inflation, demonstrating compatibility with current limits. In the heavy case, with masses well above the Hubble scale, the bispectrum exhibits a distinctive correlation between enhanced folded configurations and a `tachyonic resonance' in mildly squeezed limits, with the resonance scale set by the strength of the instability. While the main qualitative features are reproduced, we show that there exists no UV matching for which a single-field effective description, obtained by integrating out the entropic modes, accurately captures the bispectrum for all kinematic configurations. To facilitate observational applications, we introduce simple bispectrum shape templates suitable for current and forthcoming cosmological surveys. Our model-independent results allow for constraining non-standard inflationary attractors characterised by strongly non-geodesic motion.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically computes universal bispectrum signatures from transient tachyonic instabilities during inflation, revealing distinct features for light and heavy mass cases, and proposes shape templates for cosmological observations to constrain complex inflationary dynamics.
AI.motivation: Investigate universal signatures in the bispectrum caused by transient tachyonic instabilities of entropic fluctuations during inflation, which naturally occur in hyperbolic field-space geometries.
AI.method: Performed exact numerical calculations at the level of fluctuations without relying on specific background models; analyzed two mass cases (light and heavy) and computed bispectrum shapes, including application to angular inflation.
AI.result: Discovered universal magnification in folded bispectrum configurations and non-analytic scaling in the squeezed limit for light masses; identified distinctive tachyonic resonance in heavy mass cases with no single-field effective theory capturing all bispectrum features; introduced simple bispectrum templates for observational use.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a model-independent characterization of bispectrum signals from transient tachyonic instabilities, allowing constraints on non-standard inflationary models with strongly non-geodesic motion, and highlights limitations of single-field effective descriptions for heavy entropic modes.

title: The RRATalog: a Galactic census of rotating radio transients
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Rotating radio transients (RRATs) represent a significant but poorly understood component of the Galactic neutron star population, characterized by sporadic emission first detectable only through single-pulse searches. We present the RRATalog, an up-to-date catalogue of 335 RRATs, and utilize a uniform sample of RRATs discovered in four Parkes telescope surveys to model their Galactic population. Accounting in detail for observational selection effects, we find a radial density profile similar to pulsars, but identify a significantly steeper luminosity function (power-law index $α\simeq -1.3$) than previously assumed. For sources beaming towards Earth, we estimate $34000 \pm 1600$ potentially observable RRATs above a peak luminosity of 30 mJy kpc$^2$. At these high luminosities, the RRAT population is comparable in size to that of canonical pulsars. Consistent with the observed distribution, the underlying period distribution is significantly shifted toward longer periods compared to canonical pulsars, suggesting RRATs represent a more evolved population. We find evidence for a turnover in the luminosity function below 30 mJy kpc$^2$, and predict that the total number of potentially observable RRATs is $\lesssim 70,000$. Applying the Tauris \& Manchester beaming model, we estimate the total Galactic RRAT population to be $\lesssim 500,000$. The implied birth rate of $\lesssim 1.4$ RRATs per century is consistent with the Galactic core-collapse supernova rate, suggesting RRATs can be reconciled with known progenitor rates without requiring a separate evolutionary origin. We provide predictions for RRAT discoveries in ongoing and future surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an updated catalogue and population model of 335 rotating radio transients (RRATs), revealing a large, evolved Galactic population with a steeper luminosity function than pulsars. The estimated RRAT population and birth rates align with known supernova rates, suggesting RRATs are an evolutionary stage of neutron stars rather than a distinct origin.
AI.motivation: To better understand the poorly characterized population of rotating radio transients (RRATs) within the Galactic neutron star population.
AI.method: Compiled a comprehensive catalogue (RRATalog) of 335 RRATs and analyzed a uniform sample from four Parkes telescope surveys, accounting in detail for observational selection effects; modeled their Galactic spatial and luminosity distributions.
AI.result: Derived a radial density profile similar to pulsars but found a steeper luminosity function (power-law index α ≈ -1.3); estimated ~34,000 potentially observable high luminosity RRATs with periods skewed longer than pulsars; evidence for a luminosity function turnover below 30 mJy kpc²; total Galactic RRAT population estimated to be ≤500,000; birth rate consistent with Galactic supernova rates, suggesting evolutionary continuity with canonical pulsars.
AI.conclusion: RRATs represent a significant neutron star population with distinct luminosity and period characteristics indicating a more evolved state; their population and birth rates align with canonical pulsars and supernova rates, negating the need for a separate evolutionary origin; ongoing and future surveys are expected to discover more RRATs.

title: Curvature-induced electroweak symmetry breaking and phase transition of a Higgs-portal dark scalar field
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, based on the talk in the "Workshop on Standard Model and Beyond 2025" (24 Aug - 3 Sep 2025) of the Corfu Summer Institute 2025 "School and Workshops on Elementary Particle Physics and Gravity" (CORFU2025)
summary: This overview of the study arXiv:2407.18845, regarding the possibility of generating gravitational waves from a curvature-induced phase transition of a non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter field with a Higgs-portal, was showcased at the "Workshop on Standard Model and Beyond 2025" of the Corfu Summer Institute 2025. The phase transition dynamics during the transition from inflation to kination were calculated for various inflationary scales, considering both positive and negative values of the non-minimal coupling, while also examining the potential for triggering electroweak symmetry breaking. Notably, kination enhances the GW amplitudes, significantly restricting the viable parameter space. While the GW spectra follow the usual rule for high-frequencies from high inflationary scales, certain regions of the parameter space allow for a potential detection with future experiments.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates that gravitational waves from curvature-induced phase transitions in a non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter field can be amplified by kination, with some parameter regions allowing future experimental detection despite tight constraints.
AI.motivation: To explore the generation of gravitational waves (GWs) from a curvature-induced phase transition involving a non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter field with a Higgs-portal mechanism, and how inflation-to-kination dynamics affect this process.
AI.method: Analyzed phase transition dynamics during the transition from inflation to kination for various inflationary scales, considering both positive and negative non-minimal coupling values, and examined their effect on triggering electroweak symmetry breaking. Computed GW amplitudes and spectra under these conditions.
AI.result: Kination enhances gravitational wave amplitudes, strongly constraining the parameter space. While high-frequency GW spectra align with expectations from high inflationary scales, certain parameter regions predict signals potentially detectable by future experiments.
AI.conclusion: Curvature-induced phase transitions in a non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter model can produce detectable gravitational waves, especially enhanced by kination periods, but viable scenarios are limited due to stringent parameter constraints.

title: Beaming of polarized radiation in subcritical X-ray pulsars
comment: 17 pages, Selected Papers from "The Modern Physics of Compact Stars and Relativistic Gravity 2025" (Yerevan, Sept. 23-26, 2025), submitted to Particles
summary: Radiation of X-ray pulsars is powered by accretion on the neutron star surface from a binary companion under the influence of a strong magnetic field. We study beaming of this radiation in the case of subcritical X-ray pulsars, where it is formed in the accretion channel close to the neutron star surface. We solve equations of the hydrodynamics and radiative transfer of two coupled polarization modes in the accretion channel numerically, taking into account resonant Compton scattering and vacuum polarization. The beaming patterns are obtained for different accretion rates, photon energies and polarizations, and for different models of the neutron star surface radiation. The calculated beaming patterns are converted into light curves for both the intensity and polarization, taking into account the effects of General Relativity. These beaming patterns and light curves are found to be strongly affected by the resonant Compton scattering for photon energies comparable with the electron cyclotron energy. In particular, the angular redistribution of radiation near the cyclotron resonance may reduce the light-curve modulation amplitude, which is consistent with observational indications of a suppressed pulsed fraction at these energies.

AI.tldr: This paper models radiation beaming in subcritical X-ray pulsars including resonant Compton scattering and vacuum polarization, finding that scattering at cyclotron resonance reduces pulse modulation consistent with observations.
AI.motivation: Understanding the beaming of X-ray pulsar radiation, particularly for subcritical X-ray pulsars, to explain observational features such as pulsed fraction suppression.
AI.method: Numerical solution of hydrodynamics and radiative transfer equations for two coupled polarization modes in the accretion channel, including resonant Compton scattering and vacuum polarization effects; computation of beaming patterns and light curves incorporating General Relativity.
AI.result: Beaming patterns and light curves are strongly influenced by resonant Compton scattering near the electron cyclotron energy, causing angular redistribution of radiation that can reduce light-curve modulation amplitude, matching observational data showing suppressed pulsed fraction at these energies.
AI.conclusion: Resonant Compton scattering near the cyclotron resonance critically impacts the emission beaming and observed light curves of subcritical X-ray pulsars, explaining the reduced pulsed fraction in observational data.

title: Cosmological zoom-in perturbation theory as a consistent beyond point-particle approximation framework
summary: Modelling structure formation across the full dynamical range of the Universe remains a major challenge in cosmology. This difficulty originates from a fundamental limitation of geodesics in general relativity: a one-parameter family of geodesics can cease to be geodesic at a finite time. This implies that the conventional point-particle approximation is not the primary issue; rather, the breakdown of geodesic flow restricts a consistent description across scales. We develop a covariant multi-scale framework that resolves this problem by decomposing spacetime into hierarchical regions separated by matter horizons. We show how to match shared boundary consistently at the level of the action, leading to a covariant backreaction contribution. The resulting construction provides a first-principles theoretical foundation for cosmological zoom-in simulations and yields an effective energy-momentum tensor capturing the impact of the geometric backreaction effect. As an application, we demonstrate that this backreaction naturally produces flat galaxy rotation curves without invoking an additional dark matter component. Our results establish a new perspective on nonlinear structure formation, in which long dynamical range is resolved through a hierarchy of discrete geodesic domains.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a covariant multi-scale framework decomposing spacetime hierarchically to overcome geodesic breakdown issues in cosmological modeling, providing a first-principles basis for zoom-in simulations and explaining flat rotation curves without dark matter through geometric backreaction.
AI.motivation: Address the fundamental limitation of geodesic flow breakdown in general relativity that restricts consistent cosmological modeling across scales and limits the validity of the point-particle approximation in structure formation.
AI.method: The approach decomposes spacetime into hierarchical regions separated by matter horizons and matches their shared boundaries consistently at the action level, producing a covariant backreaction contribution and an effective energy-momentum tensor that captures geometric backreaction.
AI.result: Introduction of a hierarchical multi-scale formalism yielding a covariant backreaction term and demonstrating that this backreaction can explain flat galaxy rotation curves without extra dark matter, offering a new perspective on dynamical range resolution in nonlinear structure formation.
AI.conclusion: The developed covariant multi-scale framework provides a consistent theoretical foundation for modeling nonlinear structure formation across all dynamical scales of the Universe, effectively resolving the issue of geodesic breakdown and naturally explaining flat galaxy rotation curves without additional dark matter.

title: Multimessenger Constraints on Production Sites of High-Energy Neutrinos from NGC 1068
summary: The detection of high-energy neutrino signals from the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 provides us with a unique opportunity to explore nonthermal processes near the center of supermassive black holes. Using the IceCube and Fermi-LAT data, we present general multimessenger constraints on the energetics of cosmic rays and the compactness of the neutrino emission region (${\mathcal R}$), considering not only $pγ$ but also $pp$ processes. Compared to the photohadronic scenario, the hadronuclear scenario can alleviate constraints on the emission region, yielding ${\mathcal R}\lesssim30-70$ for low-$β$ plasma and ${\mathcal R}\lesssim5-50$ for high-$β$ plasma. While our results support the previous conclusion that the photohadronic scenario favors a compact corona with ${\mathcal R}\sim3-10$, these suggest the relevance of further investigations into $pp$ neutrino contributions. When the cosmic-ray spectrum is extended from 1 GeV, we find that the requred cosmic-ray luminosity exceeds the X-ray luminosity for a spectral index of $s_{\rm CR}\gtrsim2$, which challenges some shock acceleration models. We also show that the beta decay scenario is unlikely even if the magnetic field is as strong as the maximum allowed by the Eddington luminosity. Given that NGC 1068 can be established as a neutrino source, our results will provide evidence for the standard hadronic scenario, including magnetically powered corona models having hard spectra with $s_{\rm CR}\lesssim2$.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes neutrino signals from NGC 1068 using multimessenger data, showing hadronuclear processes ease constraints on emission region size and support hadronic models with hard cosmic-ray spectra, challenging some acceleration scenarios.
AI.motivation: To explore nonthermal processes near supermassive black holes by analyzing high-energy neutrino signals from NGC 1068.
AI.method: Utilized IceCube and Fermi-LAT data to constrain cosmic ray energetics and neutrino emission region compactness, considering both photohadronic ($p\gamma$) and hadronuclear ($pp$) processes.
AI.result: Hadronuclear scenarios relax constraints on emission region size compared to photohadronic ones; photohadronic favors a compact corona (${\mathcal R}\sim3-10$). Cosmic-ray luminosity requirements challenge shock acceleration models for spectral index ${s_{\rm CR}\gtrsim2}$. Beta decay scenario is unlikely under maximal magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: Findings support standard hadronic models with magnetically powered corona and hard cosmic-ray spectra (${s_{\rm CR}\lesssim2}$), highlighting the importance of hadronuclear contributions to neutrino production in NGC 1068.
